strengths: First non-asymptotic oracle complexity analysis of annealed importance sampling that does not rely on isoperimetric/log-concavity assumptions on the target — a genuinely new contribution relative to prior work (Brosse et al., 2018; Ge et al., 2020; Andrieu et al., 2016) that required such conditions.

The core proof technique is elegant and conceptually clear: comparing the ALD path measure to an optimally 'compensated' reference path measure via Girsanov's theorem, and connecting the resulting KL bound to the W2-action of the interpolation curve. This yields the clean JE result T = Θ(A/ε²) (Thm. 6) and nicely unifies the analysis with stochastic thermodynamics (dissipated work = KL(P→‖P←)), connecting to known O(1/T) variance decay results.

The lower bound in Prop. 9 (exponential action for geometric interpolation on a Gaussian mixture) is a valuable and non-obvious negative result that substantiates the paper's motivation for RDS-based curves; the accompanying Remark 23 on the W1 vs. W2 metric-derivative gap is of independent interest.

The RDS proposal (Sec. 6) with the OU-process curve is well-motivated: Prop. 10 shows the action is bounded by dβ + m² under mild assumptions, contrasting sharply with the exponential lower bound for geometric interpolation. Thm. 11 gives a clean sufficiency condition (KL(Q‖Q†) ≲ ε² and TV(π, πδ) ≲ ε).

Very thorough and self-contained appendix: detailed proofs, pseudo-code, median trick, equivalence of relative-error criterion to free-energy estimation, and a useful discussion of the error criterion relative to bias/variance. The extension results for PIS/CMCD (Props. 40–41) add value beyond the main contributions.

Careful identification of the fundamental trade-off between closed-form drift terms (geometric interpolation) and action/isoperimetric properties (OU curve) — a useful conceptual takeaway for the field.
weaknesses: The main bounds are upper bounds only, and tightness is admittedly open (acknowledged in Sec. 7). The ε⁻⁴ term in Thm. 8 (from controlling the discretization error KL(P‖P→)) looks potentially loose relative to the ε⁻² rates in equilibrium methods (Ge et al., 2020), and no lower bound is provided even for the geometric interpolation AIS setting. Without tightness, the practical significance of the complexity result is uncertain.

The complexity is expressed in terms of the action A, which is generally not computable or controllable a priori for a given target. For arbitrary non-log-concave targets, the guarantee may be vacuous, and the paper provides lower bounds only for one specific one-dimensional Gaussian mixture instance (Prop. 9).

The RDS 'framework' in Sec. 6 / App. E.5 does not deliver a complete end-to-end complexity guarantee of its own: the KL(Q‖Q†) analysis is imported wholesale from prior works (Huang et al., 2024a,b; He et al., 2024; Vacher et al., 2025), whose guarantees are exponential in d or in 1/ε. Assembling these results is useful but limits the novelty and impact of this component.

Assumption 2 is somewhat restrictive and convenient: existence of a stationary point within distance O(1/√β) of the origin is imposed 'for technical purposes,' and the paper's claim of minimal assumptions on the target should be tempered accordingly (the analysis still requires β-smoothness and this stationarity condition).

The proof of Thm. 6 explicitly builds on Guo et al. (2025, Thm. 1) and Vargas et al. (2024, Prop. 3.3), and the JE/AIS identity framework is classical (Neal 2001; Jarzynski 1997; Crooks 1998). While the synthesis and the action-based analysis are new, the incremental technical novelty relative to these works should be more clearly delineated.

No numerical experiments whatsoever. Even for a theory paper, a small-scale empirical validation (e.g., verifying the predicted behavior on Gaussian mixtures where the action is computable) would strengthen the claims about the practical inefficiency of geometric interpolation vs. OU-based curves.

Minor presentation issues: typos ('poof methodology' on p.2), some notation burden (multiple path measures P, P→, P←, P^b→, P→), and occasional proof steps left informal (e.g., the Novikov condition is assumed throughout, per Remark 16).
